title: Heaven and Earth, Praise the LORD
summary: The psalmist summons the whole created order to praise the LORD: first everything above, angels, sun, moon, stars, and the highest heavens, then everything below, sea creatures, weather, mountains, trees, animals, and every human being from kings to children. The reason is that God made them all by his command, and that he has raised up strength for his own people Israel.
story: Psalm 148 is the third of the five Hallelujah psalms that close the Psalter. Psalm 147 praised God as rebuilder of Jerusalem and ruler of the weather; Psalm 148 widens the circle as far as it can go, until nothing in heaven or on earth is left out of the choir. Yet it ends where the previous psalm did, with Israel, the people near to God. The world's praise and Israel's story belong together. The next psalm, 149, will turn to the assembly of the faithful singing a new song, and Psalm 150 will end the book with everything that has breath.
historical:
Like the other final Hallelujah psalms, Psalm 148 has no superscription, and its author and date are unknown. Nothing in its content ties it to a specific event. Many scholars place the collection of Psalms 146 to 150, and perhaps their composition, in the period after the Babylonian exile, when the Psalter was being gathered into its final five-book form; others think the hymn could be older temple praise. The reference to God raising up a horn for his people in verse 14 suggests some act of deliverance or restored strength, but the psalm does not say what it was.

The psalm had a long life in later worship. Psalms 145 to 150 became part of the Jewish daily morning prayers, and in Christian tradition Psalms 148 to 150 were sung together at the dawn office known as Lauds, whose name comes from the Latin word for praise. A long hymn in the Greek additions to Daniel, the Song of the Three Young Men, calls on sun, moon, frost, mountains, and creatures to bless the Lord in a pattern very like this psalm.
cultural:
The first hearers lived among peoples who worshiped the things this psalm lists. The sun, moon, and stars were gods or the visible bodies of gods in Egypt, Babylon, and Canaan. The great sea creatures and the ocean depths stood in many ancient myths for chaos powers that the gods had to fight. Storm and hail were the weapons of the storm god. Psalm 148 takes every one of these supposed powers and assigns it a place in the choir. They are not gods to be feared or served; they are creatures who praise the one who made them, fulfilling his word.

The list of people in verses 11 and 12 is also pointed. Kings and rulers in the ancient world were often treated as semi-divine or as the chosen sons of gods. Here they stand in the same line as young men, maidens, old people, and children. Every rank and age owes the same praise to the same God. The phrase waters above the skies (verse 4) reflects the ancient picture, also found in Genesis 1:7, of waters held above the expanse of the sky, the source of rain.
literary: The psalm has two matching halves. Verses 1 to 6 call on praise “from the heavens” and verses 7 to 14 call on praise “from the earth”. Each half ends with the same formula, “Let them praise the name of the LORD” (verses 5 and 13), followed by a reason introduced by for. The first reason is creation: God commanded and they were created, and he fixed them in place forever. The second reason is God's unique exaltation and his care for his people. Within each half the lists move roughly from high to low, and the second list moves through sea, sky, land, plants, animals, and humans in an order that recalls the creation account of Genesis 1. The Hebrew verb for praise appears again and again, driving the poem forward like a repeated drumbeat.

outline.t: Praise from the heavens: angels, hosts, lights, and skies
Because God commanded and they were created
Praise from the earth: sea, weather, land, creatures, and all people
Because his name alone is exalted and he has raised up his people

doctrines.note: Everything that exists, from angels to cattle, owes its being to God's command: he spoke and they were created, and he fixed their order by decree. The psalm leaves no room for any other power in the universe; every creature has a maker.

Verse 13 says his name alone is exalted and his splendor is above earth and heaven. Worship belongs to God, not to the sun, the sea, or the king, and the whole universe is pictured as finding its purpose in praising him.
The psalm ends not with the cosmos but with Israel, a people near to him. The God of all creation has bound himself to a particular people, and their nearness to him is the climax of the whole song.

words.note: Bara, to create. This verb has only God as its subject in its basic form in the Hebrew Bible, and it is the same verb used in Genesis 1:1. In verse 5 it grounds the whole call to praise: the heavenly bodies praise because they were created, and a creature's first duty and joy is to acknowledge its creator.

Qeren, horn. The horn of an animal like a wild ox was its weapon and the sign of its strength, so in Hebrew poetry a raised horn stands for power, victory, or honor restored. Elsewhere the image is used of a king (Psalm 132:17, of David's line). Here God has raised up strength for his people, whether a leader, a victory, or restored standing.

Chasid, saint or godly one. The word is related to chesed, God's loyal love, and describes people who belong to that love and answer it with faithfulness. Verse 14 calls Israel his chasidim, the ones whose praise he has made possible. The same word becomes important in Psalm 149.

christ: The New Testament picks up two threads from this psalm. Zechariah's song at the birth of John the Baptist blesses God for raising up “a horn of salvation” in the house of David (Luke 1:69), language that echoes verse 14 and Psalm 132 and applies it to the coming Messiah. And the vision of a whole creation praising God is realized in Revelation 5:13, where every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea praises the one on the throne and the Lamb. Paul says that all things were created through Christ and for him (Colossians 1:16), so the creation's praise in Psalm 148 is, in Christian reading, praise directed to the Father through the Son. The link is one of fulfillment and widening rather than direct prediction.

hard.q: How can mountains, hail, and cattle praise God when they have no voice or mind?
hard.a: The psalm uses a poetic figure: creatures praise God by being what he made them to be and doing what he commands. The powerful wind is described as “fulfilling His word” (verse 8), and that obedience is its praise. Psalm 19 says the same about the heavens, which declare God's glory without speech or words. Some interpreters also see in such passages a real sense in which the whole creation is oriented toward God and will share in the renewal of all things (Romans 8:19-22). Either way, the psalm isn't claiming that trees sing hymns; it is claiming that everything that exists points to its maker, and that human beings, who can speak, are called to give voice to what the whole world is already saying.

questions: The psalm puts kings and children in the same line of praise. What does that suggest about how status looks in God's presence?
Many of the things listed here were worshiped by Israel's neighbors. What created things do people treat as ultimate today, and how does this psalm put them in their place?
If creation praises God by doing what he made it to do, what would it look like for your ordinary work and life to be praise?
